newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Havel appeals to Czechs to vote for Senate.
newsitem.headline: Havel appeals to Czechs to vote for Senate.

text.p: President Vaclav Havel appealed to Czechs to vote in a Senate election run-off which began on Friday but an opinion poll said turnout was likely to be as poor as in the first round.
Havel told citizens to vote to help legitimise the newly-created Senate after only 35 percent bothered to cast ballots in the first round held on November 15-16.

"A higher turnout of voters is desirable so that the Senate can gain strong legitimacy on which it can gradually build up its authority, which is important to the balance of our constitutional system," Havel said in a statement.
The elections to the new upper house had been billed as a significant test of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's centre-right coalition, which lost its lower house majority six months ago.
Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) performed well in the first round, taking 36.5 percent of the vote compared with only 20.3 percent for the opposition Social Democrats.
But the low turnout rendered the result almost worthless for judging support for the government in a lower house election, where participation is usually much higher.
An opinion poll published on Friday forecast the run-off -- in which the first round winner and runner-up meet if no one won more than half the vote -- would not be much better attended.
The Factum poll in the daily Mlada Fronta Dnes showed that only 31 percent of respondents had decided definitely to vote while another 15 percent were considering doing so.
Analysts have blamed widespread scepticism about the need for an upper house plus an unfamiliar first-past-the-post system spread over two weekends for the voter apathy.
They add that general disgust with Czech politicians and a series of scandals involving both sides have also undermined interest in the Senate polls.

In the first round, the well-organised and well-funded ODS proved much better at getting its supporters to vote than the Social Democrats, whose leader Milos Zeman was one of the many who questioned whether the country needed a Senate.
But Zeman changed his tune when he went to vote with his wife in a Prague suburb on Friday.

"Everything depends on turnout. If two-thirds of voters stay home, it is obvious that Social Democrats will gain less Senators than if the turnout is higher," he told reporters. "I hope that participation will increase in the second round."

Zeman suffered the humiliation of having to vote for a candidate of the Christian Democrats, a junior partner in Klaus's coalition, as the Social Democrat candidate in his home constituency failed to make it to the second round.
Voting in 77 of the 81 constituencies -- four were settled in the first round -- ends at 1400 local time (1300 GMT) on Saturday and full results are expected around midnight.
